title: Mathematics as illusion
content_html:
Mathematics as illusion

Whether mathematics is an illusion depends on how we understand the relationship between human cognition and the underlying structure of reality. Here are some perspectives:

Mathematics as Discovery (Platonism)

In this view, mathematics is not an illusion but a description of eternal truths. Numbers, geometric forms, and equations exist independently of humans, and we merely discover them. For example, prime numbers or π would “exist” whether or not humans did. This perspective treats mathematics almost like a hidden realm of reality.

Mathematics as Invention (Nominalism / Formalism)

Here, mathematics is a human-constructed system of symbols and rules, like a language. We invented “2 + 2 = 4” as a consistent way to manipulate abstractions, but outside of us, “2” doesn’t exist. From this view, mathematics is closer to an illusion - powerful, yes, but no more real than the rules of chess.

Mathematics as Evolutionary Tool

Our brains evolved to perceive patterns useful for survival (quantities, symmetry, ratios). Mathematics might just be the refined extension of this instinct. In this sense, it’s not a universal truth but an adaptive map of reality - an approximation that works because the universe is structured in regularities.

Mathematics as Structure of Reality

Max Tegmark and others argue that the universe is mathematics - its very fabric is mathematical structure. If this is correct, mathematics is not an illusion at all, but the most fundamental “substance” of reality. What seems like an illusion is our limited perception of it.

Mathematics as a Collective Memory Illusion

Calling mathematics an “illusion” could also mean that it gives us the sense of certainty - an impression of timeless truth - while in fact, it is context-bound to our axioms, definitions, and proofs. Gödel’s incompleteness theorems, for example, show that even within mathematics, there are truths that cannot be proven. This undermines the illusion of mathematics as a perfectly closed, self-sufficient system.

Mathematics might be an illusion if we think it perfectly mirrors reality - it doesn’t. But it is not an illusion in terms of its utility: it consistently predicts, explains, and shapes the physical world. The “illusion” may lie in our belief that mathematics is absolute, rather than a lens through which finite minds apprehend infinite complexity.

Mathematics as Memory Stabilization

Our minds are unstable, constantly reconstructing memory rather than replaying it. Mathematics provides a stable external memory: once written, “2 + 2 = 4” doesn’t change. In this sense, mathematics is like externalized memory architecture, giving permanence to something that inside the brain is always probabilistic.

Mathematics as Consciousness Shortcut

Consciousness filters a chaotic world through simplifications. Numbers, symmetry, and equations are compressed representations of experience - efficient shortcuts, like how memory compresses past events. This creates an illusion of timelessness: mathematics feels eternal, when in fact it is our chosen reconstruction of patterns.

Mathematics as Shared Memory (Collective)

Unlike personal memory (subjective and unstable), mathematics is collective and repeatable, it functions like a cultural engram: stored outside any single mind, retrievable across generations. This is why mathematics feels more “real” than individual perception - it’s not dependent on one brain.

Illusion of Certainty

Memory often feels certain even when false. Mathematics, too, gives us the sense of certainty. But Gödel, quantum indeterminacy, and chaotic systems reveal gaps in its completeness. Thus, mathematics might be a memory illusion at scale: convincing, useful, but never perfectly aligned with reality.

Mathematics as Consciousness Mirror

Consciousness is recursive: it can observe itself. Mathematics works the same way - numbers about numbers, functions about functions. This recursion can give the illusion of infinite depth, just as memory creates an endless sense of time stretching backward and forward.

Mathematics is not “false,” but it may be an illusion in the same way memory is:

  • Selective, compressive, stabilizing, collective.
  • Useful for survival and meaning-making.
  • Giving the impression of absolute truth, while actually a dynamic reconstruction.

Memory × Mathematics × Consciousness

At the center, all three share a role as illusions of stability: they compress complexity into manageable forms, they provide continuity across time (past ↔ present ↔ future), and they give us the feeling of certainty in an unstable world.

  • Memory gives the illusion of personal continuity.
  • Consciousness gives the illusion of a unified self.
  • Mathematics gives the illusion of eternal truth.

Together, they form a triad of stabilizing illusions - not false, but functional fictions that make life, thought, and science possible.

Memory

  • Nature: Probabilistic, reconstructive, unstable.
  • Illusion: Feels like direct replay, but is actually reconstruction.
  • Stabilizing Function: Gives continuity of self across time.
  • Connection to Mathematics: Both externalize and systematize patterns, turning unstable mental traces into reliable structures.

Consciousness

  • Nature: Filtering, binding, recursive self-awareness.
  • Illusion: Feels unified and constant, though it’s fragmented and fluctuating.
  • Stabilizing Function: Creates the sense of a single “observer.”
  • Connection to Mathematics: Both impose structure on chaos, generating clarity and order from flux.

Mathematics

  • Nature: Abstract, symbolic, rule-bound.
  • Illusion: Appears eternal and universal, but depends on human concepts and cultural scaffolding.
  • Stabilizing Function: Provides certainty, reproducibility, and collective memory.
  • Connection to Memory: Mathematics is “externalized memory” - stored outside brains, stable across generations.
  • Connection to Consciousness: Gives the mind recursive tools to reflect on itself (logic, infinity, paradox).

Mathematical Universe Hypothesis

The Mathematical Universe Hypothesis (MUH) is a bold proposal by physicist Max Tegmark that says reality itself is a mathematical structure. Not just that mathematics describes the universe well, but that the universe is mathematics at its core. In physics, equations and models often seem to “fit reality” astonishingly well (e.g., Maxwell’s equations for electromagnetism, Einstein’s relativity equations, Schrödinger’s equation for quantum mechanics). Tegmark takes this further: the reason math works so well is because physical reality and mathematical structure are identical. In other words, the universe does not have mathematics - it is mathematics.

Tegmark links MUH to a “multiverse hierarchy”:

  • Level I: Infinite space → different regions look different but obey the same laws.
  • Level II: Different physical constants or laws (inflationary cosmology).
  • Level III: Many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics.
  • Level IV (MUH): All mathematically possible structures exist as universes.
  • Our universe is just one particular mathematical structure.
  • Other universes correspond to other self-consistent mathematical systems.

If MUH is true, “existence” = “mathematical consistency.” - conscious beings are just patterns within mathematical structures, and there is no need for “substance” beyond maths; the physical is nothing but the mathematical. However, MUH may be untestable; it risks being more philosophy than physics. Just because we observe a mathematical universe doesn’t prove all structures exist - maybe only “life-friendly” ones do? What does it mean for a purely abstract structure to “exist”? Is mathematical existence the same as physical existence? If MUH is right, then memory and consciousness are patterns within a mathematical object, amd our “illusion of continuity” (memory reconstructing identity, consciousness selecting inputs) would itself be part of the deeper structure of mathematics. That would mean even the instability of memory is “hard-coded” as part of the mathematical structure we inhabit.

The Mathematical Universe Hypothesis says that the universe isn’t described by math, it literally is math - a self-consistent structure among infinitely many. It’s elegant but controversial: it explains why mathematics works so well, but at the cost of turning physics into metaphysics.

Platonism

Platonism is the belief that mathematical objects exist independently of us, in a non-physical, timeless realm. Numbers, sets, geometric forms, and other mathematical entities are not human inventions - they are discovered, not created. Example: the number π existed long before humans, and would still “exist” if humanity disappeared.

Plato argued that beyond the physical world of appearances lies a realm of Forms (Ideas), perfect and eternal. For Plato, things like circles or triangles in the physical world are imperfect copies of the true Form of Circle or Form of Triangle. In modern mathematics, Platonism extends this idea: mathematical truths belong to the realm of Forms.

  • Universality: mathematics works the same for everyone, everywhere.
  • Stability: 2 + 2 = 4 is true regardless of culture or time.
  • Effectiveness: the success of math in physics (Wigner’s puzzle) is no surprise if reality is mathematical at its core.

Critiques:

  • Epistemology problem (Benacerraf’s problem): If numbers exist in a non-physical realm, how do we know about them? What’s the “causal link”?
  • Ontological extravagance: Do we really need to believe in a mysterious “realm” of mathematical objects to explain math’s success?

Alternative accounts:

  • Formalism: math is just symbol manipulation.
  • Nominalism: math is invented, not discovered.
  • Structuralism: what exists are structures and relations, not “objects” themselves.

Like memory, Platonism creates the illusion of permanence and certainty in a world of change. Just as memory “reconstructs” continuity of self, Platonism “posits” continuity of truth in a separate realm. Consciousness, too, feels unified and eternal - a parallel to how Platonism sees mathematical truths. Platonism holds that mathematical entities are real, timeless, and independent of human thought. It explains universality and effectiveness but raises deep puzzles about how finite beings could access such an eternal realm.
